Fully Flexible Probabilities

Flexible empirical distributions and Entropy Pooling in R.

Empirical distributions are often built from historical scenarios that receive equal probability. This is a natural starting point when there is no reason to consider some scenarios more plausible than others.

In practice, however, we may have additional information. Fully Flexible Probabilities provide a way to incorporate this information without changing the scenarios. Only the probability attached to each scenario is allowed to change.

ffp organizes this process into a model workflow. You define the scenario support, choose prior probabilities, express views about the distribution, and use Entropy Pooling to obtain posterior probabilities that satisfy those views while remaining as close as possible to the prior.

Installation

Install the released version from CRAN with:

install.packages("ffp")

You can install the development version from GitHub with:

# install.packages("pak")
devtools::install_github("Reckziegel/FFP")

A model-first workflow

Consider 500 simulated scenarios for equity returns, bond returns, and inflation.

library(ffp)

set.seed(123)

scenarios <- tibble::tibble(
  equity    = rnorm(500, mean = 0.006, sd = 0.04),
  bonds     = rnorm(500, mean = 0.002, sd = 0.012),
  inflation = rnorm(500, mean = 0.025, sd = 0.007)
)
scenarios
#> # A tibble: 500 × 3
#>      equity     bonds inflation
#>       <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 -0.0164  -0.00522    0.0180 
#>  2 -0.00321 -0.00992    0.0177 
#>  3  0.0683   0.0143     0.0249 
#>  4  0.00882  0.0110     0.0241 
#>  5  0.0112  -0.0161     0.00715
#>  6  0.0746   0.000858   0.0323 
#>  7  0.0244  -0.00875    0.0267 
#>  8 -0.0446  -0.0228     0.0419 
#>  9 -0.0215   0.00380    0.0298 
#> 10 -0.0118   0.00105    0.0219 
#> # ℹ 490 more rows

Each row represents one possible scenario. At this point, the data describe what can happen, but we have not yet specified how probable each scenario should be.

Define the scenario support

The first step is to create an ffp model from the scenarios.

model <- ffp_model(scenarios)

ffp_model() defines the support of the empirical distribution. These scenarios remain fixed throughout the Entropy Pooling workflow.

Choose a prior

Next, we specify the probabilities we want to assign before incorporating any views.

A uniform prior gives every scenario the same initial probability.

model <- model |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  )

The prior represents what we believe about the scenarios before introducing additional information.

Add a view

Suppose we believe that the expected equity return should be 1%. We express this directly as a view on the model.

model <- model |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = 0.01)
  )

A view describes a property that we want the posterior distribution to satisfy. Here, it concerns the posterior mean of equity.

Fit the model

Finally, we combine the prior and the view using Entropy Pooling.

fit <- ffp_fit(model)
fit
#> <ffp_fit>
#> Scenarios:      500
#> Views:          1
#> Status:         converged
#> KL divergence:  0.00226086
#> Max residual:   6.66e-16

ffp_fit() finds posterior scenario probabilities that satisfy the view while remaining as close as possible to the prior in relative-entropy terms. The scenario support remains unchanged; only the probabilities are updated.

Once the individual steps are familiar, the same model can be written as a single pipeline:

fit <- scenarios |>
  ffp_model() |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  ) |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = 0.01)
  ) |>
  ffp_fit()

Understanding the posterior

Because the fitted model retains both the scenarios and their prior and posterior probabilities, distributional changes can be inspected directly.

stats <- ffp_stats(fit)
stats
#> <<ffp_stats>>
#> Prior -> posterior empirical distribution
#> 
#> Scenarios: 500
#> Variables: 3
#> Tail probability: 1.0%
#> 
#> Effective scenarios
#> Prior ENS: 500.0 (100.0%)
#> Posterior ENS: 498.9 (99.8%)
#> ENS retained: 99.8%

To understand what happened to a particular variable:

summary(stats, variable = "equity")
#> <summary_ffp_stats>
#> Variable: "equity"
#> 
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   statistic             prior posterior    change
#>   <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 mean                0.00738    0.0100  0.00262 
#> 2 sd                  0.0389     0.0390  0.000110
#> 3 skewness            0.0861     0.0818 -0.00430 
#> 4 kurtosis            2.95       2.94   -0.0145  
#> 5 quantile           -0.0830    -0.0803  0.00269 
#> 6 expected_shortfall -0.0924    -0.0904  0.00201

Tail risk can be inspected using the usual loss convention:

ffp_risk(fit, confidence = 0.99)
#> <ffp_risk>
#> Prior -> posterior tail risk at 99.0% confidence
#> 
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   variable  value_at_risk_prior expected_shortfall_prior value_at_risk_posterior
#>   <chr>                   <dbl>                    <dbl>                   <dbl>
#> 1 equity                0.0803                   0.0924                  0.0803 
#> 2 bonds                 0.0233                   0.0277                  0.0245 
#> 3 inflation            -0.00978                 -0.00801                -0.00978
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: expected_shortfall_posterior <dbl>
#> 
#> Prior ENS: 500.0
#> Posterior ENS: 498.9
#> ENS retained: 99.8%

The same posterior probabilities can therefore be used to study changes in location, dispersion, shape, tail risk, and the effective number of scenarios.

Priors and views

A uniform prior is only the simplest starting point.

ffp can construct priors from time decay (prior_exp_decay()), rolling windows (prior_rolling_window()), market conditioning (prior_crisp()), custom probabilities (prior_custom()), or combinations of different prior specifications (prior_product()).

prior_exp_decay(half_life = 60)
prior_kernel(inflation, target = 0.03, bandwidth = 0.005)

Views can describe different features of the posterior distribution.

view_mean(equity, target = 0.01)
view_probability(inflation > 0.04, target = 0.20)
view_quantile(equity, target = -0.08, level = 0.05)

Several views can be attached to the same model and processed jointly.

Partial confidence

ffp_fit() computes the full-confidence Entropy Pooling posterior.

When a view should influence the distribution without being imposed with full confidence, the prior and full-confidence posterior can subsequently be combined through opinion pooling.

pooled <- ffp_opinion_pooling(fit, confidence = 0.75)
pooled
#> <ffp_opinion_pool>
#> Scenarios:   500
#> Confidence:  75%

View confidence is a modeling choice and is distinct from numerical solver tolerances.

ffp 2.0

ffp 2.0 introduces a higher-level, model-first interface built around ffp_model(), ffp_prior(), ffp_view(), and ffp_fit().

Lower-level probability, view, and Entropy Pooling functions remain available, but the model workflow is the recommended starting point for new analyses.
